title: What manner of love (1 John 3:1–3)
hookLine: see what love: that we should be called children of God

cards: Somewhere in a lot of families there's a box: crayon drawings, a first shoe, a report card, a lock of hair.
Plenty of people only find it as adults, clearing out a closet, and it stops them cold: someone kept all of this, because it was mine. A love they never saw, kept the whole time.

Today's passage is three verses long, and it begins with that kind of surprise. The writer has been talking about light and darkness, sin and commandments. Then he stops, as if overcome, and says: look.

teach.h: BEHOLD: WHAT KIND OF LOVE IS THIS?
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God." Behold: look at this.
What manner of love: the Greek phrase carries surprise, something like, what kind of love is this? Bestowed is a gift word. Not earned.
And the gift is a name: called children of God. A detail from the manuscripts: the oldest Greek manuscripts add three more words, and so we are. Called children of God, and so we are.
The manuscripts behind the King James didn't have them, and modern translations usually put them back. It's as if the writer worried someone would think called was only a title. It's what you are.
Then why the world doesn't always see it: "therefore the world knoweth us not, because it knew him not." If people missed who Jesus was, they'll miss his children too.

teach.h: NOW, BUT NOT YET WHAT WE SHALL BE.
teach.b: Then the future, and what he admits he doesn't know: "Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be." Already, but not yet finished.

teach.h: WE SHALL SEE HIM AS HE IS.
teach.b: What he does know is that when he appears, "we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is."
And the last verse says hope like that changes how you live now: whoever has this hope purifies himself.

how: Many Christians read 1 John 3:1–2 at baptisms and on All Saints' Day, and the line about seeing God as he is shapes Christian hope in Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant teaching alike.

o: paid back after a long debt
given as a gift, not earned

games.q: what's inside 1 John 3:1–3 — tap the pairs.
p: words found in the oldest manuscripts

s: the KJV includes the words 'and so we are' in 3:1
the manuscripts behind the KJV lacked them. the oldest Greek manuscripts have them.
the writer admits we don't yet know what we shall be
"it doth not yet appear what we shall be."
being called children of God is only a title here
the writer insists: called, and so we are.

games.q: you're the writer. you've just said believers are called children of God. how do you make sure no one hears it as only a title?
o: explain what a name means in law.
games.why: the oldest manuscripts read, called children of God, and so we are. not only a name: a fact.

practice: Notice the names you call yourself in a hard moment, failure, too much, not enough, without arguing with them.
Then set beside them the name the letter uses, children of God, with your own name in front of it if you pray, or a plainer one if that phrase isn't yours: I am loved. Rest there, and just look.

wordCard.voice: Bestowed. First John's gift word, not earned, but given: the Father's love that lets us be called children of God, and so we are.

orig.note: Greek: what kind of, what sort of, often with a note of wonder. the word behind 'what manner of'.

carryVoice: Your line: children of god. Called, and so we are. That's day six hundred eighty-five.
